comparisons.peer_summary: The firm uses a consistent historical simulation VaR model based on a three-year historical window, with a primary statistic at a 99% confidence level and one-day holding period, simulating portfolio value under various scenarios.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Bank of America disclose their primary VaR model methodology and scope for trading portfolios. Citi utilizes a Monte Carlo simulation model to capture material risk sensitivities across various asset classes, explicitly excluding AFS and HTM investment securities. In contrast, Bank of America uses a consistent historical simulation approach based on a three-year historical window with a 99% confidence level and one-day holding period. While both models aim to measure market risk in trading portfolios, they differ in simulation technique (Monte Carlo vs. Historical Simulation), confidence levels (Citi's specific level is not defined in the text but BAC uses 99%), and data windows (Citi uses market factors, BAC uses a three-year historical window).

sentences.text: Citi uses a single, independently approved Monte Carlo simulation VaR model (see "VaR Model Review and Validation" below), which has been designed to capture material risk sensitivities (such as first- and second-order sensitivities of positions to changes in market prices) of various asset classes/risk types (such as interest rate, credit spread, foreign exchange, equity and commodity risks).
Citi's VaR includes positions that are measured at fair value; it does not include investment securities classified as AFS or HTM.
We use one VaR model consistently across the trading portfolios and it uses a historical simulation approach based on a three-year window of historical data.

Our primary VaR statistic is equivalent to a 99 percent confidence level, which means that for a VaR with a one-day holding period, there should not be losses in excess of VaR, on average, 99 out of 100 trading days.

comparisons.peer_summary: The company uses a single VaR model with a one-day time horizon and 95% confidence level to estimate potential loss from adverse market movements in interest rates, equity, currency, and commodity prices, facilitating portfolio comparison and capturing firmwide diversification.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Goldman Sachs use a single VaR model to capture market risks for their portfolios. Citi employs an independently approved Monte Carlo simulation model to capture first- and second-order sensitivities. Goldman Sachs also uses a single VaR model but specifies a one-day time horizon with a 95% confidence level to estimate potential loss from adverse market movements in interest rates, equity, currency, and commodity prices. Both disclosures highlight the use of a unified model approach for risk measurement, though they differ in the specific simulation method (Monte Carlo for Citi, unspecified method for GS) and confidence levels (95% for GS).

comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and JPMorgan describe their VaR model framework as capturing material market risks through granular calculations. Citi uses a single, independently approved Monte Carlo simulation VaR model designed to capture material risk sensitivities across various asset classes. JPMorgan utilizes granular individual VaR models that simulate historical market returns for individual risk factors and product types, aggregating results at the Firm level. Both disclosures emphasize the use of specific models to capture material risks arising from market factors, with Citi focusing on a unified Monte Carlo model and JPMorgan focusing on granular individual models aggregated at the firm level.

sentences.text: Citi uses a single, independently approved Monte Carlo simulation VaR model (see "VaR Model Review and Validation" below), which has been designed to capture material risk sensitivities (such as first- and second-order sensitivities of positions to changes in market prices) of various asset classes/risk types (such as interest rate, credit spread, foreign exchange, equity and commodity risks).

These VaR models are granular and incorporate numerous risk factors and inputs to simulate daily changes in market values over the historical period; inputs are selected based on the risk profile of each portfolio, as sensitivities and historical time series used to generate daily market values may be different across product types or risk management systems.

comparisons.peer_summary: The VaR model uses a one-year equal-weighted historical simulation for general market risk and Monte Carlo simulation for name-specific risk, constructing a distribution of hypothetical daily portfolio value changes based on historical market factor movements and sensitivities.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Morgan Stanley employ Monte Carlo simulation within their VaR modeling frameworks. Citi uses a single, independently approved Monte Carlo simulation VaR model to capture material risk sensitivities. Morgan Stanley uses Monte Carlo simulation specifically for name-specific risk in bonds, loans, and related derivatives, alongside historical simulation for general market risk. Both firms incorporate Monte Carlo techniques to estimate potential losses, though Morgan Stanley's approach is hybrid (historical and Monte Carlo) while Citi's is singularly Monte Carlo.

sentences.text: Citi uses a single, independently approved Monte Carlo simulation VaR model (see "VaR Model Review and Validation" below), which has been designed to capture material risk sensitivities (such as first- and second-order sensitivities of positions to changes in market prices) of various asset classes/risk types (such as interest rate, credit spread, foreign exchange, equity and commodity risks).

We estimate VaR using a model based on a one-year equal-weighted historical simulation for general market risk factors and name-specific risk in corporate equities and related derivatives, and Monte Carlo simulation for name-specific risk in bonds, loans and related derivatives.
